question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

INTREPID
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Dauntless.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Intrepid (adjective) means fearless in the face of danger; showing resolute courage. (निडर, साहसी)
◦ Example: The intrepid climbers reached the summit despite the blizzard.

 

• Dauntless carries exactly this sense — not to be discouraged or intimidated by difficulty or danger. (अडिग, निर्भीक)
◦ Example: Her dauntless defence of the proposal won over the committee.

 

• Both words are built on a negative prefix: in- (not) + trepidus (alarmed) gives intrepid; daunt (to intimidate) + -less gives dauntless. Spotting the negation is the fastest route to the answer.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Timorous (डरपोक, भीरु): showing or suffering from nervousness and fear — the opposite of intrepid.

 

• Option 2: Craven (कायर): contemptibly cowardly — also an antonym.

 

• Option 4: Cowardly (डरपोक): lacking courage — again an antonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Note the pattern used here: three antonyms and one synonym. SSC alternates between this arrangement and its reverse, so always fix the meaning of the given word before scanning the options.

 

• Other synonyms of intrepid: valiant, undaunted, audacious, doughty, stouthearted.

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.

 

A storm in a teacup
option_1: A great commotion over a trivial matter
option_2: A sudden and violent quarrel between friends
option_3: A brief period of calm before serious trouble
option_4: A secret plan hatched among a few people
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. A great commotion over a trivial matter.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "A storm in a teacup" means a great deal of anger, excitement or fuss about something very unimportant. (राई का पहाड़ बनाना)
◦ Example: The dispute over the seating arrangement turned out to be a storm in a teacup.

 

• The image is that of a tempest confined to a vessel small enough to hold in one hand — violent in appearance but negligible in scale. The American form of the same idiom is "a tempest in a teapot".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 describes a real quarrel; the idiom specifically implies that the matter was not worth the quarrel.

 

• Option 3 describes an interval of quiet, for which the expression would be "the calm before the storm" — the commonest trap in this question.

 

• Option 4 describes a conspiracy, nearer to "to hatch a plot".

 

NOTE

 

• Idioms of exaggeration frequently asked in SSC: "To make a mountain out of a molehill", "Much ado about nothing", "To cry wolf" and "To split hairs" (to argue over insignificant details).

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

GREGARIOUS
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Reclusive.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Gregarious (adjective) means fond of company; sociable. Of animals, it means living in flocks or herds. (मिलनसार, यूथचारी)
◦ Example: A gregarious student, he knew half the hostel within a week.

 

• Its true opposite is reclusive — avoiding the company of others; living in seclusion. (एकांतप्रिय)
◦ Example: The poet grew reclusive in his later years and refused all invitations.

 

• The word comes from Latin grex, gregis (a flock) — the same root as congregate, aggregate and segregate.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Sociable (मिलनसार): enjoying the company of others — a direct synonym.

 

• Option 2: Convivial (आनंदप्रिय): cheerful and friendly, especially in company — also a synonym.

 

• Option 3: Affable (सुशील, मृदुभाषी): easy to talk to and pleasant in manner — again a synonym.

 

NOTE

 

• Other antonyms of gregarious: solitary, withdrawn, unsociable, introverted, aloof.

 

• Do not confuse reclusive (living apart from society) with exclusive (restricted to a select few) — a pair SSC has set against each other before.

question: Identify the misspelt word from the given options.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Mischievious.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct spelling is "Mischievous" — causing or inclined to cause playful trouble or minor harm. (शरारती)
◦ Example: The mischievous child hid his sister's spectacles.

 

• Spelling key: MIS + CHIEV + OUS. The word has only three syllables — mis-chie-vous — and there is no "i" before the final "-ous". The error arises from mispronouncing it as four syllables, on the pattern of devious and previous.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Rhythm (लय) — correctly spelt; note that it contains no vowel except the "y".

 

• Option 2: Silhouette (छायाकृति) — correctly spelt; a French borrowing with a silent "h" and a double "t".

 

• Option 4: Camouflage (छद्मावरण) — correctly spelt; also from French, ending in "-flage".

 

NOTE

 

• Other words commonly given an extra syllable in error: grievous (not grievious), heinous (not heinious), disastrous (not disasterous) and remembrance (not rememberance).

question: Spot the correct spelling of the scientific measurement of the depth of oceans and other water bodies.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Bathymetry.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Bathymetry" is the measurement and mapping of the depth of oceans, lakes and other bodies of water — in effect, the study of underwater topography. (जल-गहराई मापन)
◦ Example: Detailed bathymetry of the continental shelf was prepared before the pipeline was laid.

 

• Break the word into its Greek roots: BATHY (deep) + METRY (measurement). The same roots appear in bathysphere (a deep-sea diving vessel) and in geometry, symmetry, telemetry.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "Bathimetry" — incorrect; the root is "bathy" with a y, not "bathi".

 

• Option 2: "Bathymetery" — incorrect; an extra "e" has crept into the suffix, which is "-metry".

 

• Option 3: "Bathometry" — incorrect; "batho" is not the form used in this word.

 

NOTE

 

• Related measurement terms worth remembering: altimetry (height), anthropometry (human body measurements), audiometry (hearing) and hypsometry (land elevation).

question:
Choose the correct one-word substitute for the given expression.

 

'A system of government in which religious leaders rule in the name of divine authority'
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Theocracy.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A theocracy is a state governed by priests or religious leaders who claim to rule on behalf of a deity, with religious law serving as the law of the land. (धर्मतंत्र)
◦ Example: In a theocracy, religious doctrine takes precedence over civil legislation.

 

• The word is formed from Greek theos (god) + kratos (rule, power). The same root theo- appears in theology, atheist and monotheism.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Autocracy (निरंकुश शासन): government by one person holding unlimited power.

 

• Option 3: Technocracy (तकनीकीतंत्र): government by technical experts such as scientists and engineers.

 

• Option 4: Gerontocracy (वृद्धतंत्र): government by the elderly.

 

NOTE

 

• The "-cracy" family is a standing favourite in SSC: democracy (people), aristocracy (nobility), plutocracy (the wealthy), bureaucracy (officials), meritocracy (the able), kleptocracy (thieves) and ochlocracy (the mob).

 

• Note the parallel "-archy" family: monarchy (one ruler), oligarchy (a few), anarchy (no ruler) and matriarchy/patriarchy.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

Not until the final witness had testified ___ the true sequence of events.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. did the jury understand.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• When a sentence opens with a negative or restrictive expression such as "Not until", "Never", "Seldom", "Rarely", "Only after" or "Under no circumstances", the main clause must undergo inversion — the auxiliary is placed before the subject.

 

• The structure is: Not until + subordinate clause + auxiliary + subject + main verb.

◦ Correct: Not until the final witness had testified did the jury understand the true sequence of events.
◦ Example: Only after the results were declared did he realise his mistake.

 

• Note that the inversion applies to the main clause, not to the not until clause itself, which keeps normal word order.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 uses normal statement order, which is not permitted after an opening negative expression.

 

• Option 3 adds an emphatic "did" but keeps the subject first, so the required inversion still does not occur.

 

• Option 4 inverts correctly but uses the past perfect, which clashes with the past perfect already used in the not until clause.

 

NOTE

 

• Remember the two-clause rule: in Hardly had he arrived when …, No sooner had he arrived than … and Not until … did he …, only one clause is inverted — the one beginning with the negative word.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

The minister's reply was a masterpiece of ___; it committed the government to nothing at all.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. ambiguity.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The blank follows the preposition "of", and a preposition must be followed by a noun (or a gerund). Only "ambiguity" is a noun.

 

• Ambiguity means the quality of being open to more than one interpretation; lack of definiteness. (अस्पष्टता, द्व्यर्थता)
◦ Example: The clause was rewritten to remove the ambiguity about the deadline.

 

• The second clause — it committed the government to nothing at all — confirms the sense: the reply was deliberately open-ended.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: ambiguous is the adjective (an ambiguous reply) and cannot follow of.

 

• Option 2: ambiguously is the adverb (he replied ambiguously).

 

• Option 4: ambiguate is not a word in standard English.

 

NOTE

 

• Word-form questions are decided by what precedes the blank: after a/an, the, of, in, with a noun is required; after is, was, seems, appears an adjective; and modifying a verb, an adverb.

 

• Learn the full set for common roots: clarity / clear / clearly, brevity / brief / briefly, obscurity / obscure / obscurely.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

 

Repeated postponements of the hearing have begun to ___ public confidence in the tribunal.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. erode.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Erode" means to wear away gradually, and in its figurative use it is the standard verb for the slow weakening of abstract things such as confidence, trust, authority, credibility and support. (धीरे-धीरे क्षीण करना)
◦ Example: The delay in paying salaries eroded the staff's trust in the management.

 

• The clue lies in "repeated postponements" — a gradual, cumulative process, which is exactly what erode denotes.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: corrode (क्षरित करना): to destroy metal gradually by chemical action. Figuratively it suggests something eating into the mind, as in jealousy corroded their friendship, but it is not used with confidence.

 

• Option 2: abrade (घिसना): to scrape or wear away a physical surface by rubbing.

 

• Option 3: dissolve (घुलना): to pass into solution, or to formally bring an assembly to an end — the House was dissolved.

 

NOTE

 

• Fixed collocations worth memorising: erode confidence/authority; undermine a position; shake someone's faith; restore trust; command respect.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

The villagers complained that they (1)/ had been deprived (2)/ from the benefits of the welfare scheme (3)/ for more than three years. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (3).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The error is one of preposition. The verb "deprive" is always followed by "of", never by "from".

◦ Corrected sentence: The villagers complained that they had been deprived of the benefits of the welfare scheme for more than three years.
◦ Example: The accused was deprived of his voting rights for six years.

 

• The trap works because "from" feels natural with the idea of something being taken away. In English, however, the preposition is fixed by the verb, not by the sense.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct — complained that is the right structure, and the pronoun they agrees with the villagers.

 

• Part (2) is correct — the past perfect passive "had been deprived" rightly shows a state existing before the complaint.

 

• Part (4) is correct — "for" is properly used with a duration of time.

 

NOTE

 

• Fixed verb–preposition pairs frequently tested by SSC: deprived of, accused of, suspicious of, comprised of (avoid), prevented from, prohibited from, differ from, congratulate on, insist on, rely on, comply with, familiar with and conform to.

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error.

 

What the auditors objected to most strongly (1)/ were the absence of supporting vouchers (2)/ for the expenses incurred (3)/ during the last quarter of the year. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. (2).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The subject of the sentence is the noun clause What the auditors objected to most strongly. A noun clause beginning with "what" is always treated as singular, so the verb must be "was", not "were".

 

• The complement here — "the absence" — is itself singular, which confirms the choice.

◦ Corrected sentence: What the auditors objected to most strongly was the absence of supporting vouchers for the expenses incurred during the last quarter of the year.
◦ Example: What we need is more time, not more money.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct — object to takes the preposition to, which is properly retained at the end of the clause.

 

• Part (3) is correct — the expenses incurred is a well-formed past-participle phrase.

 

• Part (4) is correct — during is the right preposition for a stretch of time.

 

NOTE

 

• The rule holds even when the complement is plural in careful writing: What we need is more books. Where the complement is plural and the sense is genuinely plural, some writers use are, but SSC follows the singular rule.

 

• Compare the related structure: "All that glitters is not gold" — a that-clause subject also takes a singular verb.

question:
Change the following sentence from active voice to passive voice.

 

Complete the application form in block letters.
option_1: The application form must complete in block letters.
option_2: Let the application form be completed in block letters.
option_3: The application form is being completed in block letters.
option_4: Let the application form completed in block letters.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Let the application form be completed in block letters.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The given sentence is an imperative — it gives an instruction and has no stated subject.

 

• The passive of an affirmative imperative is formed as: Let + object + be + V3.
◦ Active: Complete the application form.
◦ Passive: Let the application form be completed.
◦ Example: Shut the door → Let the door be shut.

 

• For a negative imperative, the pattern is Let + object + not be + V3: Do not disturb the files → Let the files not be disturbed.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is active in form and ungrammatical — a form cannot "complete" itself.

 

• Option 3 turns the instruction into a statement in the present continuous passive, losing the imperative force altogether.

 

• Option 4 omits "be", which is essential to the structure Let … be … V3.

 

NOTE

 

• Where the imperative is a request or advice, the passive may instead use "You are requested to …" or "… should be …": Please help the candidates → You are requested to help the candidates.

question:
Convert the sentence given below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure.

 

A gold medal was awarded to the winner by the governor.
option_1: The governor was awarded a gold medal to the winner.
option_2: The winner awarded a gold medal to the governor.
option_3: The governor awarded the winner a gold medal.
option_4: A gold medal awarded the winner by the governor.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The governor awarded the winner a gold medal.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb "award" takes two objects — an indirect object (the person: the winner) and a direct object (the thing: a gold medal). Such verbs can be made passive in two ways, and here the direct object has been made the subject.

 

• To restore the active voice: bring the agent after "by" to the front as the subject, and place the two objects after the verb.
◦ Passive: A gold medal was awarded to the winner by the governor.
◦ Active: The governor awarded the winner a gold medal.

 

• The tense — simple past — is carried over unchanged, and the preposition "to" is dropped when the indirect object comes immediately after the verb.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is still passive in structure and also makes the governor the recipient.

 

• Option 2 reverses the roles entirely — the winner becomes the giver.

 

• Option 4 has no auxiliary and no logical subject, so it is not a complete sentence.

 

NOTE

 

• Verbs with two objects — give, offer, award, send, teach, promise, lend, pay, show — allow two passives:
◦ The winner was awarded a gold medal. (indirect object made subject)
◦ A gold medal was awarded to the winner. (direct object made subject)

question:
Select the sentence that contains the homophone of the highlighted word.

 

The chef received a warm compliment from the visiting guests.
option_1: She paid him a compliment on his punctuality.
option_2: The dry white wine was a perfect complement to the fish.
option_3: His compliment pleased the entire kitchen staff.
option_4: The review closed with a compliment to the pastry section.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The dry white wine was a perfect complement to the fish.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A homophone is a word that sounds the same as another but is spelt differently and has a different meaning. (समोच्चारित किंतु भिन्न वर्तनी वाला शब्द)

 

• Compliment (with an i) means an expression of praise or admiration.
• Complement (with an e) means something that completes or goes well with another thing; it is also used for a full quantity, as in the ship's complement of officers. The two are pronounced alike, so "complement" is the homophone required.

◦ Example: The two schemes complement each other rather than overlap.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Options 1, 3 and 4 all reuse the same spelling "compliment" in the sense of praise, so none of them supplies a homophone.

 

NOTE

 

• Memory aid: compliment contains i — I like to praise; complement contains e — it enhances or completes.

 

• Note also the adjectives: complimentary means praising or given free of charge, while complementary means completing, as in complementary angles.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

Of all the forms of pollution, the one that has spread fastest and provoked the least protest is the loss of darkness. A child born in a large Indian city today may reach adulthood without ever having seen the Milky Way, which was visible from almost every rooftop within living memory. The change has been quick as well as quiet: measurements of the night sky suggest that it grows brighter by several per cent each year, a rate that would double the glow within a single generation.

 

Unlike smoke or effluent, artificial light is not a by-product that anybody regrets. It is the thing itself, deliberately produced and widely welcomed, and it carries a powerful argument in its favour: lit streets are believed to be safe streets. The belief is only partly borne out. Studies of street lighting and crime return mixed results, and the glare thrown by badly aimed fixtures can actually reduce what a passer-by is able to see. What is beyond dispute is that a great deal of the light we generate never reaches the ground at all. It is flung sideways and upwards, illuminating nothing but the underside of the atmosphere.

 

The biological costs are becoming clearer. Migratory birds, which navigate partly by the stars, are drawn off their routes and exhausted by lit towers. Insects gather and die around lamps they seem unable to leave. Sea turtle hatchlings, which move instinctively towards the brightest horizon, crawl inland towards roads instead of seawards.

 

What makes this problem unusual is that it is among the very few that can be reversed within hours rather than decades. A shielded lamp, aimed downwards and set to a warmer colour, costs no more than an unshielded one and consumes less electricity. Nothing has to be invented, and nothing that anyone values has to be surrendered. The darkness returns the moment we stop wasting the light.

 

What does the author mean by the phrase "illuminating nothing but the underside of the atmosphere"?
option_1: That artificial light has begun to alter the composition of the air
option_2: That much of the light escapes upwards and serves no purpose on the ground
option_3: That the atmosphere reflects light back to the earth at night
option_4: That streetlamps are deliberately aimed at the sky for safety
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. That much of the light escapes upwards and serves no purpose on the ground.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sentence just before the phrase states the point plainly: a great deal of the light we generate never reaches the ground at all, being flung sideways and upwards.

 

• The phrase is therefore an ironic description of waste — the light does illuminate something, but only the sky, which nobody needs lit. The word "nothing but" carries the irony.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 introduces a chemical change to the air, which the passage never suggests.

 

• Option 3 describes reflection back to earth, whereas the author's complaint is that the light is lost.

 

• Option 4 is contradicted by the passage, which blames badly aimed fixtures, not deliberate skyward lighting.

 

NOTE

 

• For figurative-phrase questions, read the sentence immediately before the phrase. Authors normally state the idea plainly first and then restate it in an image.

How does the author describe the pace at which the night sky is growing brighter?
option_1: Rapid enough to double the glow within a single generation
option_2: Slow but steady over several centuries
option_3: Uneven, with long periods of no change at all
option_4: Rapid in villages but negligible in cities
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Rapid enough to double the glow within a single generation.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The first paragraph states that the night sky grows brighter by several per cent each year, and adds that this is a rate that would double the glow within a single generation.

 

• The author reinforces the point with a concrete illustration: a child born in a large Indian city today may reach adulthood without ever having seen the Milky Way, which was visible from rooftops within living memory.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 contradicts the passage, which stresses that the change has been quick.

 

• Option 3 introduces an unevenness the author never mentions.

 

• Option 4 reverses the geography — the passage's example is drawn from a large city.

 

NOTE

 

• Where a passage gives a figure and then restates it in plainer terms ("several per cent each year" → "double within a generation"), the restatement is usually what the option reproduces. Match the idea, not the number.

Nothing has to be invented, and nothing that anyone values has to be surrendered. The darkness returns the moment we stop wasting the light.

 

Why, according to the passage, is artificial light dangerous to sea turtle hatchlings?
option_1: The heat of the lamps damages their shells
option_2: Bright light prevents them from hatching at night
option_3: They mistake lamps for the moon and stop moving altogether
option_4: They move towards the brightest horizon and so crawl inland
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. They move towards the brightest horizon and so crawl inland.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The third paragraph states that sea turtle hatchlings move instinctively towards the brightest horizon and therefore crawl inland towards roads instead of seawards.

 

• The instinct itself is sound — in the natural world the brightest horizon is the open sea. Artificial lighting simply reverses which direction is brighter, so the same instinct now leads them the wrong way.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 mentions heat, which the passage does not discuss.

 

• Option 2 refers to hatching, whereas the passage describes what happens after hatching.

 

• Option 3 says they stop moving; the passage says they keep moving, but in the wrong direction.

 

NOTE

 

• The paragraph lists three effects in parallel — on migratory birds, insects and turtle hatchlings. SSC often builds one option out of the wrong item in such a list, so match the example named in the question.

What makes this problem unusual is that it is among the very few that can be reversed within hours rather than decades. A shielded lamp, aimed downwards and set to a warmer colour, costs no more than an unshielded one and consumes less electricity. Nothing has to be invented, and nothing that anyone values has to be surrendered. The darkness returns the moment we stop wasting the light.

 

Which of the following best captures the central theme of the passage?
option_1: Street lighting has failed to reduce urban crime
option_2: Wildlife should be given priority over human convenience
option_3: Light pollution is a widespread harm that is unusually easy to reverse
option_4: Cities should reduce their consumption of electricity at night
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Light pollution is a widespread harm that is unusually easy to reverse.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage has two halves. The first establishes the scale of the harm — a fast-spreading pollution that provokes no protest, with measurable costs to birds, insects and turtles.

 

• The last paragraph supplies the other half: this is among the very few problems that can be reversed within hours rather than decades, since a shielded lamp costs no more and uses less electricity. Option 3 captures both halves.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 takes up a single supporting detail — the mixed evidence on lighting and crime — and mistakes it for the theme.

 

• Option 2 sets wildlife against people, a conflict the author expressly denies by noting that nothing that anyone values has to be surrendered.

 

• Option 4 is a by-product of the author's remedy, not its purpose.

 

NOTE

 

• A central-theme option must cover the whole passage. Reject any option that is true of only one paragraph, however accurately it reports that paragraph.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

Of all the forms of pollution, the one that has spread fastest and provoked the least protest is the loss of darkness. A child born in a large Indian city today may reach adulthood without ever having seen the Milky Way, which was visible from almost every rooftop within living memory. The change has been quick as well as quiet: measurements of the night sky suggest that it grows brighter by several per cent each year, a rate that would double the glow within a single generation.

 

Unlike smoke or effluent, artificial light is not a by-product that anybody regrets. It is the thing itself, deliberately produced and widely welcomed, and it carries a powerful argument in its favour: lit streets are believed to be safe streets. The belief is only partly borne out. Studies of street lighting and crime return mixed results, and the glare thrown by badly aimed fixtures can actually reduce what a passer-by is able to see. What is beyond dispute is that a great deal of the light we generate never reaches the ground at all. It is flung sideways and upwards, illuminating nothing but the underside of the atmosphere.

 

The biological costs are becoming clearer. Migratory birds, which navigate partly by the stars, are drawn off their routes and exhausted by lit towers. Insects gather and die around lamps they seem unable to leave. Sea turtle hatchlings, which move instinctively towards the brightest horizon, crawl inland towards roads instead of seawards.

 

What makes this problem unusual is that it is among the very few that can be reversed within hours rather than decades. A shielded lamp, aimed downwards and set to a warmer colour, costs no more than an unshielded one and consumes less electricity. Nothing has to be invented, and nothing that anyone values has to be surrendered. The darkness returns the moment we stop wasting the light.

 

What is the tone of the author in the closing paragraph?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Constructive and hopeful.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The closing paragraph turns from the problem to the remedy. Its key statements are that the harm can be reversed within hours rather than decades, that a shielded lamp costs no more and uses less electricity, and that nothing has to be invented.

 

• The final sentence — the darkness returns the moment we stop wasting the light — is an assurance, not a lament. The tone is therefore optimistic and solution-oriented.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is the opposite of the paragraph's plain claim that the problem is easily reversible.

 

• Option 3 overstates the mood — the author assigns no blame in this paragraph and names no culprit.

 

• Option 4 ignores the clear evaluative language (unusual, nothing has to be surrendered), which shows the author is not neutral.

 

NOTE

 

• Tone questions are answered from word choice, not subject matter. A passage about damage may still close in a hopeful tone. Useful tone words for SSC: critical, satirical, ironic, nostalgic, optimistic, cautionary, objective, indignant and reflective.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

It is high time we start planning for the next academic session.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. started.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The expressions "It is high time", "It is time" and "It is about time" are followed by the simple past tense, even though the meaning refers to the present or future. This is an instance of the unreal past.

◦ Corrected sentence: It is high time we started planning for the next academic session.
◦ Example: It is high time the department published the revised syllabus.

 

• The construction carries a note of mild reproach — it implies that the action should already have been taken.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: start — the present tense is not used after it is high time.

 

• Option 2: will start — the future is never used in this structure, despite the future sense.

 

• Option 4: are starting — the present continuous is equally inadmissible here.

 

NOTE

 

• Other unreal past structures that take a past form for a present meaning: "I wish I knew…", "If only he were here…", "as if / as though he were…", "would rather you came…" and "suppose we left now".

 

• The alternative to It is high time we started is the infinitive form "It is high time for us to start".

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence.

 

Being a holiday, the office remained closed throughout the day.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. It being a holiday.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A participle must have a clear subject, and unless a subject of its own is supplied, it attaches itself to the subject of the main clause. As written, Being a holiday attaches to "the office", which absurdly says that the office was a holiday. This error is called a dangling or unrelated participle.

 

• The remedy is to give the participle its own subject, producing an absolute phrase: "It being a holiday, the office remained closed." Here It is the subject of being, and the office remains the subject of the main clause.

◦ Example: The weather being fine, we decided to walk.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 repeats the original dangling participle.

 

• Option 2: "Been a holiday" is not a usable form — the past participle cannot open a clause in this way.

 

• Option 3: "Having been a holiday" still supplies no subject, so the participle continues to dangle.

 

NOTE

 

• Classic examples of the dangling participle in SSC papers:
◦ Walking down the road, a snake bit him. → As he was walking down the road, a snake bit him.
◦ Being very hot, I opened the window. → It being very hot, I opened the window.

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

He said to me, "Where have you kept the duplicate file?"
option_1: He asked me where had I kept the duplicate file.
option_2: He asked me where I had kept the duplicate file.
option_3: He asked me where I have kept the duplicate file.
option_4: He asked me that where I had kept the duplicate file.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. He asked me where I had kept the duplicate file.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reported sentence is a Wh- question. Its rules of conversion are:

◦ The reporting verb said to changes to asked / enquired of.
◦ The question word ("where") itself serves as the conjunction — no that and no if/whether is added.
◦ The question order is dropped: the sentence takes normal statement order, subject before verb.
◦ The question mark disappears, and the tense is backshifted: have kept → had kept.
◦ The pronoun changes: you → I, matching the listener.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 keeps the interrogative order (where had I), which is not permitted in indirect speech.

 

• Option 3 fails to backshift the tense — have kept should become had kept after the past reporting verb.

 

• Option 4 wrongly inserts "that" in addition to the question word. Using both is a double conjunction and is always wrong.

 

NOTE

 

• Two patterns to keep apart:
◦ Yes/No question → asked + if / whether: "Are you ready?" → He asked whether I was ready.
◦ Wh- question → asked + the question word: "Why are you late?" → He asked why I was late.

question:
A sentence is provided in indirect speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding direct speech.

 

The visitor requested the guard to open the side gate.
option_1: "Please open the side gate," said the visitor to the guard.
option_2: "Open the side gate," the visitor ordered the guard.
option_3: "Will you open the side gate?" said the visitor to the guard.
option_4: "You should open the side gate," said the visitor to the guard.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. "Please open the side gate," said the visitor to the guard.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reporting verb "requested … to" is the standard indirect form of an imperative expressing a request. Restoring the direct speech requires the reverse of the usual rules:

◦ The infinitive "to open" is turned back into the base imperative "open".
◦ Because the reporting verb was requested, the courtesy word "Please" (or Kindly) is restored.
◦ The reporting verb becomes the neutral "said to", and the words are enclosed in inverted commas.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 uses "ordered", which would correspond to the indirect form ordered the guard to open — a command, not a request.

 

• Option 3 turns the request into a question, whose indirect form would begin asked whether ….

 

• Option 4 uses "should", giving advice rather than making a request; its indirect form would be advised the guard that he should ….

 

NOTE

 

• Match the reporting verb to the sense of the imperative: ordered/commanded for an order, requested for a request, advised for advice, begged/entreated for an entreaty, warned for a warning and forbade for a prohibition.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. The panchayat had been petitioning for six years to get a bus to stop at Dhanora.

 

A. Every application came back with the same remark: the road was too narrow for a bus to turn.

 

B. Two winters later the first bus pulled in, the widening having been done by the villagers themselves.

 

C. A retired surveyor living in the village measured the road and found that only one bend was actually too tight.

 

D. He drew up a plan showing that forty feet of a single field would settle the matter, and its owner agreed to give the strip.

 

S2. Dhanora now has four services a day, and the stop carries the name of the man who gave the land.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. A-C-D-B.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – A – C – D – B – S2. The paragraph follows an effort → obstacle → investigation → solution → outcome order.

 

• S1 states the effort — six years of petitioning.

◦ A supplies the obstacle: every application was rejected on the ground that the road was too narrow. The phrase every application points straight back to the petitioning in S1.
◦ C is the investigation — the surveyor's measurement, which directly answers the objection raised in A by showing that only one bend was the problem.
◦ D must follow C, since "He" can only be the surveyor introduced there.
◦ B gives the outcome — the bus finally arrives — and leads into the present-day scene in S2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (C-A-D-B) brings in the surveyor before the reader knows what problem he is investigating.

 

• Option 3 (A-D-C-B) lets "He" in D appear before the surveyor has been mentioned.

 

• Option 4 (C-D-A-B) places the rejection of the applications after the solution has already been found.

 

NOTE

 

• Two tests settle this question at once: the pronoun test (He in D requires C before it) and the problem-before-solution test (an objection must be stated before it is answered).

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. The postage stamp began as the answer to a problem that had little to do with convenience.

 

A. Rowland Hill proposed that the sender pay instead, at a single flat rate, proof of payment being a small adhesive label.

 

B. Until the 1840s it was the recipient of a letter who paid the charge, which varied with distance and was often simply refused.

 

C. A refused letter had cost the post office the whole journey and earned it nothing at all.

 

D. Letters were soon being posted in such numbers that the lower rate was carrying far more of them than anyone had predicted.

 

S2. Within twenty years almost every postal system in the world had copied the arrangement.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. B-C-A-D.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – B – C – A – D – S2. The paragraph moves from old practice → the problem it created → the reform → the result.

 

• S1 announces that the stamp solved a problem, without saying what it was.

◦ B names the old practice — the recipient paid, and often refused. It must come first, since everything else refers back to it.
◦ C states the problem that practice created: a refused letter cost the post office everything and earned nothing. The words a refused letter pick up often simply refused in B.
◦ A supplies the reform — Hill's proposal that the sender pay instead. The word "instead" is decisive: it can only follow a description of what was being replaced.
◦ D gives the result and leads into the worldwide adoption in S2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (C-B-A-D) mentions a refused letter before refusal has been introduced.

 

• Option 2 (B-A-C-D) places the reform before the problem it was meant to solve, leaving C stranded.

 

• Option 4 (A-B-C-D) opens with "instead", which has nothing to refer back to.

 

NOTE

 

• Words of replacement or contrast — instead, rather, on the contrary, by contrast — can never open the jumbled set. They must follow whatever is being replaced or contradicted, and spotting one usually fixes half the order immediately.
